items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we are given the equation [MATH: 3^{3x} = 81^{x-1},] which has two exponential terms. How do we solve it?

Content:
To solve this equation, we need both exponential terms to have a common base. To do this, we rewrite the equation using the fact that [MATH: 81 = {\color{red}3}^4,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: {\color{red}3}^{3x}=\left({\color{red}3}^4\right)^{x-1}]

Content:
Then, we apply the power rule for exponents:
[MATH: 3^{3x}|= 3^{4(x − 1)}]

Content:
Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base [MATH: ({\color{red}3}),] we equate the exponents and solve for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: 3x|= 4(x − 1); 3x|= 4x − 4; x|= 4]

Content:
Whenever we can rewrite an equation so that both sides have a common base, we can solve the equation by equating the exponents.

To do this, we write [MATH: 9] as [MATH: {\color{red}3}^2,] and then rewrite the right-hand side using the power rule for exponents:

[MATH: 3^{3x − 3}|= 9^{x}; 3^{3x − 3}|= (3^{2})^{x}; 3^{3x − 3}|= 3^{2x}]

Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base [MATH: ({\color{red}3}),] we equate the exponents and solve for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: \left({\color{red}3}^2\right)^{3x}=\left({\color{red}3}^3\right)^{x+2}]

Then, we apply the power rule for exponents:

[MATH: 3^{2(3x)} = 3^{3(x + 2)}]

Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base [MATH: ({\color{red}3}),] we equate the exponents and solve for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 2(3x)|= 3(x + 2); 6x|= 3x + 6; 3x|= 6; x|= 2]
